newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Outcome of EU probe into Danish ship aid unclear.
newsitem.headline: Outcome of EU probe into Danish ship aid unclear.

text.p: The European Commission's probe into Danish shipbuilding aid will not be completed before the end of this month and it is too early to say whether too much state support had been granted, an EU source said on Tuesday.
The European Union executive had not yet completed its analysis of the complicated dossier, the source told Reuters.
"It is an extraordinary complex case," he said.

He was commenting on a report in Danish financial daily Borsen which said that the Commission's competition officials had found that Denmark had violated EU rules on shipbuilding aid and that illegal state support should be paid back.
However, the source said "it is far too early for them to make that kind of assumption."

The Commission, which vets state aid in the 15-nation EU, had not yet reached any position "in relation to how many, if any, of the cases might have infringed the ceiling," he added, referring to the maximum amount of aid which governments may grant to shipyards under EU rules.
But the Commission would demand repayment if it concluded that excessive support had been granted, the source said.
Last July, the Commission announced it was starting a probe into Danish shipbuilding aid, fearing that subsidies might have exceeded EU limits between 1987 and 1993.
EU rules allow aid of up to nine percent of contract value.
The investigation was launched following the publication of a critical independent study accusing the government of illegalities.

The study, commissioned by the Danish industry ministry and carried out by accountancy firm Coopers & Lybrand, criticised changing Danish governments for subsidising the sector to the tune of four billion crowns ($672 million) over the last decade.
The Commission said then there were indications that in 65 cases vessels were financed on the basis of an inflated price level, creating a risk that the aid ceiling had been exceeded.

The study, commissioned by the Danish industry ministry and carried out by accountancy firm Coopers & Lybrand, criticised changing Danish governments for subsidising the sector to the tune of four billion crowns ($672 million) over the last decade.
However, in September Danish Industry Minister Mimi Jacobsen presented a ministry report concluding that the administration of shipbuilding aid from 1986 to 1995 complied with EU rules.
Jacobsen, who resigned in December in a government reshuffle, said she was dropping a planned legal probe into shipbuilding aid, rejecting the findings of the Coopers & Lybrand study.
She said her ministry had studied 308 cases of aid granted to Danish shipyards and found that the report's critical stance was full of errors and misinterpretations of EU rules.
Despite this, the Commission said it would complete its probe. -- Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
